newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Stock slump hits 1996 profits of S.Korean banks.
newsitem.headline: Stock slump hits 1996 profits of S.Korean banks.

text.p: Profits of South Korean commercial banks have taken a battering from big losses on the stock market, and the central bank said on Thursday any recovery depended largely on a share rebound.

The Bank of Korea, the central bank, said combined net profits of the nation's 25 commercial banks fell 2.4 percent to 846.8 billion won ($997.4 million) last year from 867.6 billion won a year earlier due to losses from stock investments.
"A slump in the stock market is mainly to blame for the decline," Lee Suk-keun, deputy drector at the central bank's supervisory planning division, told Reuters.
"A key factor for banks' performance will be the stock market this year."
In a statement, the central bank said losses from the banks' stock holdings were estimated at 4.96 trillion won in 1996, up sharply from 2.16 trillion won in 1995.
As a result, reserves for losses rose to 895.2 billion won last year from 543.7 billion in 1995, it said.

The composite stock index closed 1996 at a year low of 651.22 points, down 23.2 percent from 882.94 at the start of the year. It finished on Thursday at a provisional 711.86, up 12.10 points, or 1.73 percent, from Wednesday.

A jump in interest income helped banks report a 16.2 percent rise in operating profits to 4.17 trillion won in 1996 from 3.59 trillion in 1995, the central bank said. Interest income went up 25.2 percent to 7.31 trillion won from 5.84 trillion.
Lee said an expansion of operating funds through rights issues contributed to the rise in interest revenue.
Analysts also said banks shifted their loan strategy to the high-yielding household sector from companies on fears an economic slowdown would raise the risk on corporate borrowings.
Home loan interest rates averaged about 12-13 percent in 1996 against about 10 percent for companies.

"In addition, margins between lending and deposit rates improved as companies chased for bank loans after it became difficult to raise funds in the sagging stock market," said Bong Won-kil, an analyst at Daishin Economic Research Institute.
The central bank said provisions for non-performing loans declined 6.6 percent to 1.51 trillion won in 1996 from 1.62 trillion in 1995.
Analysts said the provision would continue to fall as losses from non-performing loans were quickly squared off. They were unable to give figures.
The central bank said non-interest income dropped 13.6 percent to 1.77 trillion won in 1996 from 2.05 trillion in 1995.
Of the 25 banks, 15 nationwide banks earned 653.5 billion won in net profits last year, down 3.7 percent from 1995. Ten regional banks netted 193.3 billion won, up 2.2 percent.
Kookmin Bank topped the list of net and operating profits with 163.6 billion won, up 60.5 percent from 1995, and 503 billion won, up 41.3 percent, respectively.

The central bank also said it would cut the bank reserve ratio by 1.5-2.0 points from the current 5.5 percent during the first quarter of this year as part of financial reforms aimed at improving competitiveness. It also plans to abolish a ceiling on the issue of certificates of deposit in the first quarter.
